senses.gloss:
Haragaurī
(‘Śiva and पार्वती’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Kālikāpurāṇa, गौरी or पार्वती, the divine spouse of शिव, once expressed a desire that she should always be with him even as a shadow is, with its original. When शिव suggested that he could give half of his body to her and that she should do the same to him, गौरी bowed down to him, to ब्रह्मा, to विष्णु and then merged half of her into his. Thus the हरगौरी form took shape. It is the same as Ardhanārīśvara.
See ARDHANĀRĪŚVARA also.

Harappa
------------------------------------------
See INDUS VALLEY CIVILISATION.

Haridāsa, Svāmī
(‘servant of Hari or विष्णु’)
------------------------------------------
Many great musicians of India—of the ancient and the medieval periods—were saints since, to them, मुसिच् was a mode of sādhanā (spiritual practice), an aspect of भक्तियोग. One such musician-saint was Svāmī Haridāsa (16th century) who was the गुरु or teacher of Tānsen, the famous court-musician of Akbar (A. D. 1556-1605).
Not much is known of him. He belonged to the निम्बार्क school of वैष्णविस्म् and lived mostly in वृन्दाबन्. Some devotional songs composed by him are still extant.

Haradatta
------------------------------------------
Haradatta (A. D.1200?) has carved out for himself an important niche in the dharmaśāstra literature. He was the second son of Padmakumāra and in all probability belonged to South India. He was a great devotee of शिव.
His works are: Anākulā, a commentary on the Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtras; Anāvilā, a commentary on the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtras; Mitākṣarā, a commentary on the Gautama Dharmasūtras; Ujjvalā, a commentary on the Āpastamba धर्म-sūtras.
These commentaries being meticulous about grammar also have been considered as models for commentators.
In philosophical conviction, he was an advaitin.

Harivyāsadeva
------------------------------------------
Nimbārka (12th century A. D.) was one of the great teachers of वैष्णविस्म् whose philosophy was known as ‘Dvaitā-द्वैत.’ हरिव्यासदेव (15th century A. D.) was an important teacher of this school. He was a disciple of the musician-saint Śrībhaṭṭa. He used to live mostly in Vṛndāvan (in the मथुरा district, Uttar Pradesh), his favorite resort being the Nāradṭīlā (Nārada’s mound) near मथुरा.
Deeply devoted to Lord कृष्ण, he was very fond of पिल्ग्रिमगे, spreading the cult of भक्ति through discourses and written compositions as also organising the people for assisting him in this task of uplifting धर्म.
It is said that, to make the Hindu society more virile, he propagated the worship and mantrajapa of नरसिṁह, the fierce aspect of Lord विष्णु. He is also believed to have stopped animal sacrifice in some देवी temples in the Himālayan region.
He has left a Sanskrit commentary on the work Vedāntaratnamañjūṣā of Puruṣottamācārya, a famous teacher of the निम्बार्क school.
His disciple Svabhūrām worked hard in the Punjab region to bring about peace among the warring factions of certain Hindu cults. Another disciple of his, Paraśurāmadeva, successfully countered the anti-Hindu activities of the Muslim fakīrs of the time.

Harihara
(‘Viṣṇu and शिव’)
------------------------------------------
Though God is one and can be worshipped through various forms and various names, this principle is often forgotten by the devotees of the various deities. This results in mutual conflicts, disturbing the social fabric and peace. Hence great saints have often made serious attempts at reconciliation of the various sects, sometimes using ingenious means. The ‘Harihara’ and the ‘Ardha-nārīśvara’ deities seem to be such innovations.
Harihara—also called Haryardha-mūrti and Śaṅkaranārāyaṇa—is Hara (Śiva) on the right side and Hari (Viṣṇu) on the left side.
The right half may be shown as red or white in complexion and has a half of the third eye on the forehead. The two right hands hold the trident or the mṛga (deer) and show the abhayamudrā.
The left half is dark in complexion, has yellow silk robes, and the hands hold the शङ्ख (conch) and गदा (mace). Sometimes चक्र (discus) and पद्म (lotus) are shown instead of the conch and the mace.
According to the Vāmanapurāṇa विष्णु is said to have revealed this form to the gods who had approached him to know where शिव was.
As per another version a demon, Guhāsura by name, had obtained a boon from ब्रह्मा that neither Hari nor Hara should be able to kill him. Hence Hari and Hara joined together in this form and killed him. The place where this manifestation took place is called ‘Harihara.’ It is an important town in the Chitradurga district of Karnataka and has a beautiful temple of शङ्कर-नारायण (same as हरिहर).
Icons of this form seem to be of great antiquity (A. D. 100) and belong to the Kuśāna period.

harijans
(‘people of God’)
------------------------------------------
This word was coined by Mahātmā Gāndhī (A. D. 1869-1948) with regard to those people in the Hindu society who had been treated for centuries as untouchables. Even if the society disowned them, God did not, since they belonged to God!—This seems to be the idea behind the word.
See ANTYAJA and ASPṚŚYATĀ.

Harivaṁśa
------------------------------------------
The Harivaṁśa is considered as the खिल part (an appendix or addendum) of the great epic Mahābhārata. Its main purpose seems to be to supply the details of the कृष्ण story, especially of the childhood and the boyhood days.
It is sometimes classed among the उपपुराणस् also, since it contains the five well-known characteristics of a standard purāṇa (vide PURĀṆAS).
It has three sections, each section being designated as a ‘parva’.
The following are the details:
Parva Chapters Verses
Harivaṁśaparva 55 3,111
Viṣṇuparva 128 7,817
Bhaviṣyatparva 135 5,205
Total 318 16,133

However, in the Critical Edition of the Mahābhārata, the details are as follows:
Harivaṁśaparva chs. 1-45; ślokas 2442.
Viṣṇuparva chs. 46-113; ślokas 3426
Bhaviṣyatparva chs. 114-118; ślokas 205
Total 118 chs. 6073 ślokas

When the people of गोकुल were not willing to go to Vṛndāvana as suggested by कृष्ण, he created a very large number of wolves from his own body to frighten them and force them to leave (2.9).
In the गोवर्धन hill episode, the description of इन्द्र’s defeat is less ignominious to him!
The incident of taking away the पारिजात tree from svargaloka (heaven) has also been described in a similar vein.
The Bhaviṣyatparva contains the following stories: जनमेजय’s sacrifice, च्रेअतिओन् of the world by God, episode of the king पृथु, destruction of दक्ष’s sacrifice, stories of some of the avatāras or incarnations of विष्णु, शिव and कृष्ण, कृष्ण’s killing of several demons and so on.

Haridās, Sādhu
------------------------------------------
Haridās was a well-known disciple of श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य or चैतन्य Mahā-prabhu (A. D. 1485-1533). He was a Muslim by birth. He was born probably in A. D. 1450 in the village Burhan in the Jessore district of Bengal (now in Bangladesh). Right from young age he had a great fascination for Hindu religion and that too, for Lord Śrī कृष्ण. He came under the influence of चैतन्य महाप्रभु and became his disciple.
When attempts were made by evil and jealous persons to seduce him with the help of a harlot, it was she who was converted to purer ways of living! So great was his self-control and devotion to Lord कृष्ण.
The Muslim chieftain of the place made several attempts to reconvert him to Islamic way of life but failed miserably. Finally Haridas was beaten to pulp and thrown into the river nearby. However, due to the grace of God he survived.
It is said that चैतन्य himself cremated his body on his death.

Hargobind, Guru
(A. D. 1595-1644)
------------------------------------------
No society, however great its religion and culture, can survive sans a righteous military power to protect it from external or internal aggression. The Hindu society should be extremely grateful to the Sikh movement led by its great Gurus, which provided such a protection, in its critical moments.
One such person was the sixth गुरु, Hargobind, the harbinger of Sikh militarism. He showed by his life and deeds, how a balanced combination of kṣāttra (heroic) and brāhma (saintly) spirits can work in the best interest of a society.
He was born in A. D. 1595 as the son and successor of गुरु Arjan (A. D. 1564-1606). He became the गुरु in A. D. 1606. It is said that at the time of installation as the गुरु, he refused to accept his ancestral necklace and turban and declared that his swordbelt—with two swords symbolising both spiritual and temporal supremacy which he called miri and piri—was his necklace and aigrette. This was the first step towards the transformation of सिखिस्म् into a militant church.
The first corps of Sikh volunteers was raised by him at Amritsar. The first battle against the Mughal forces had already been fought in A. D. 1628. गुरु Hargobind further strengthened his Sikh forces. It is said that he had seven hundred horses in his stables, had trained three hundred cavaliers and sixty artillery men.
However, he was essentially a saint and Samarth Rāmadās is reported to have been inspired by him to fight against the oppression of the aliens.
Establishing sanctuaries for travellers and restoring leprosariums was also an important task undertaken by him.
During his tenure as the गुरु, सिखिस्म् spread beyond the borders of India also.
Tegh Bahādūr (A. D. 1621-1675), the ninth गुरु, was Hargobind’s surviving son.

Haridāsas, of Karnataka
------------------------------------------
See DĀSAKŪṬA.

Harkiṣan, Guru
(A. D. 1656-1664)
------------------------------------------
That spiritual greatness need not and does not depend upon the physical age of a person has been proved time and again in the lives of many a saint—whether it is शुक of the paurāṇik age or Jñāndev (13th Century) of the historic age. गुरु Harkiṣan, the eighth in the line of the Sikh Gurus, belongs to this category.
When the seventh गुरु, Har Rai (A. D. 1630-1661), chose his second son Harkiṣan for the august seat of the Sikh Gurus, he was hardly five years old! However, like the early morning sun which, though small, lights up the whole world, गुरु Harkiṣan shone in his precocious wisdom of explaining the Ādi Granth, the basic scripture of the Sikhs.
Rām Rai, his elder brother, who had been superseded in favour of his younger brother, complained to the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb (A. D. 1618-1707) and sought his assistance to redress the ‘injustice’ done to him. When the emperor called गुरु Harkiṣan to his court and tried to test him, the child-गुरु acquitted himself admirably.
Smallpox which was raging at Delhi at that time, took the life of the young गुरु at the tender age of eight.
Before passing away he nominated Teg Bahādur of the town Bakālā as the next गुरु.

Haridvāra
(‘gateway to [God] Hari’)
------------------------------------------
Haridvāra (also spelt as Haradvāra and Hardwar) is one of the most famous places of पिल्ग्रिमगे associated with and on the bank of the river गङ्गा. Since it is the gateway as it were, to the two well-known places of पिल्ग्रिमगे in the हिमालयस्, viz., बदरीनाथ and केदारनाथ, sacred to Hari (Viṣṇu) and Hara (Śiva), it is but proper to christen it as ‘Haridvāra’ and ‘Haradvāra’.
गङ्गा">Banks of the river GaṅgāIt is situated at a distance of 263 kms. (164 miles) from New Delhi, on the right bank of the river गङ्गा at the foot of the Siwalik range of the हिमालयस्, in the Saharanpur district of Uttaranchal.
As per the various accounts given in the पुराणस्, it is one of the seven most sacred places of पिल्ग्रिमगे, known as Māyāpurī in the ancient days. It was here that सती, the spouse of Lord शिव, gave up her body in योग, during the sacrifice performed by her ड़थेर् दक्ष. The sages कपिल, भरद्वाज and Sanatkumāra lived here. अर्जुन and भीम, the famous Pāṇḍava heroes had visited this place.
Greater हरिद्वार comprises Hari-द्वार proper, Māyāpurī, कनखल, Jvālāpura and Bhīmagouḍ, which are different areas in and around the place. Hṛṣīkeśa (Hrishikesh), 40 kms. (24 miles) away from हरिद्वार, is a famous place of residence for many saṁnyāsins who have established their hermitages and practise austerities and spiritual studies.
The main attraction of हरिद्वार is the Brahmakuṇḍa, the place where pilgrims take bath in the गङ्गा. There is a temple of the river goddess Gaṅgādevī called ‘Prācīna-गङ्गा-mandira’ and the ārati in the evening, at sunset time, is very spectacular, with hundreds of oil lamps set afloat on the river by the devotees. It is here that the pilgrims take their bath during the कुम्भमेला (See KUMBHAMELĀ for details.) which takes place once in twelve years when बृहस्पति (Jupiter) enters the Meṣarāśi (Aries).
The bathing ghāṭ at Kuśāvarta is the place where the pilgrims offer पिण्ड (rice balls) to their ancestors.
The temple of Bilvakeśvara, the कनखल-kuṇḍa (tank for taking bath), Saptadhārākuṇḍa (another tank), the temples of Śravaṇanātha, Viṣṇupāda, ईश्वर, गणपति, Caṇḍikā, Gaurīśaṅkara and Dakṣeśvara as also the Saptarṣi आश्रम are the other places of importance for the pilgrims to visit.

Haritālikā
------------------------------------------
Vratas (religious vows) and utsavas (festivals) are an important aspect of Hindu rituals.
The हरितालिका which falls on the third day of the bright fortnight (śukla tṛtīyā) of the month of Bhādrapada (generally September) is a popular vrata observed by the Hindu women (whose husbands are alive), mostly in Maha-rashtra and Rajasthan. It is performed to please Umā or पार्वती, the spouse of शिव, to secure health and longevity for their husbands. ड़स्तिन्ग्, worship of Umā with शिव and breaking the fast after the मोओन् is seen are part of this vrata.
A grand procession of an image of पार्वती taken out from the city palace of Mahārājā Mān Singh in Jaipur, is a special feature of this festival.

Haridrā-Gaṇapati
(‘Gaṇapati [of yellow complexion like] turmeric powder’)
------------------------------------------
Gaṇapati is a very popular deity in हिन्दुइस्म् even today. One of the important forms worshipped in the tāntrik cults is हरिद्रा-गणपति. He is described as yellow in complexion and clad in yellow garments. He has six arms carrying पाश (noose), aṅkuśa (goad) and परशु (axe) in three hands. The other three exhibit the abhaya (protection), varada (boon-giving) and krodha (indignation) mudrās or poses.
For purposes of worship, the icon can be prepared in powdered turmeric also.
Since the word ‘niśā’ (= रात्रि or night) is another name for ‘haridrā’, this aspect of गणपति is also referred to as ‘Rātri-गणपति’.

Hārīta
------------------------------------------
Hārīta is an ancient sage mentioned by भीष्म in the Mahābhārata (Śāntiparva ch. 278) as having taught a गीता now known as the Hārītagītā. The contents of the Hārītagītā, which has just 22 verses and describes the code of conduct for a saṁnyāsin can be summarised as follows:
A sādhaka or a mumukṣu (one who is desirous of लिबेरतिओन्) should first renounce the world and take to the saṁnyāsin’s life. He should not find fault with others. He should be friendly and kind towards all. He should bear with fortitude all insults that may be hurled at him by others. He should approach the householders for alms after they have finished their ड़ोओद्. He should eat just enough to keep the body and the सोउल् together. He should resort to lonely places for contemplation on the आत्मन्. He should practise self-control at all times. He should be broad-minded, always detached from the things of the world and never harm anybody. Such an one will attain the world of light, the highest Abode.
Hārīta is also the name of a famous writer of धर्मसूत्रस् who has often been quoted by other ancient authors like आपस्तम्ब and वसिष्ठ as an authority. Though his time is not known, he existed long before A. D. 600.
From the profuse quotations given by other writers of the धर्मशास्त्रस्, some scholars have tried to rebuild his lost work.
The Dharmasūtras of हारीत was definitely an extensive work, in prose and verses. The topics as gleaned from the quotations given in others are as follows: sources of धर्म, two kinds of brahma-cārins, the स्नातक, the गृहस्थ (householder), the vānaprasthin (forest hermit), injunctions and prohibitions about ड़ोओद्, अशौच (ceremonial impurity), śrāddha (obsequial rites), पञ्चमहायज्ञस् (five daily sacrifices), Vedic studies, statecraft, court procedures, sins and expiations, prayers and so on.
Hārīta refers to two kinds of women: brahmavādinīs and sadyovadhūs. The former were entitled for उपनयन, Vedic studies and keeping the sacred fire.
Two more works, one known as Laghu-Hārīta and the other as Vṛddha-Hārīta are mentioned by some writers like अपरार्क (12th century A. D.).

Har Rāi, Guru
(A. D. 1630-1661)
------------------------------------------
Har Rāi was the seventh गुरु of the Sikhs. He was the son of Bābā Gurudittā and grandson of गुरु Hargobind. Sulakhaṇī was his noble and worthy wife.
Once he saw गुरु Hargobind (A. D. 1595-1644) from a distance and while rushing to meet him, broke some branches of a flower plant. This pained him so much that he started weeping. Observing this, the गुरु advised him with a few words that became the beacon of his life.
Guru Hargobind nominated him as his successor in 1644 before his death.
Guru Har Rāi kept up the military traditions introduced by his गुरु Hargobind for the defence of धर्म. It is said that he had 2200 armed followers.
There were no armed conflicts during his time with the ruling powers.
He established three important teaching missions. They were by Bhagvān Gir (or Bhagat Bhagvān), Saṅgatīā (or Bhāī Pherū) and Bhāī Gondā. These preachers worked respectively in eastern India, western India and Kābūl. Two more preachers—Bhāī Natthā and Bhāī Jodh—were also sent to preach at Ḍhākā and Multān.
He normally lived at Kirātpur and kept the daily practices of his predecessors.
Dārā Shukoh, elder brother of Aurangzeb had sought the blessings of गुरु Har Rāi. This enraged Aurangzeb who asked the गुरु to come and meet him. But the गुरु cleverly avoided it and sent instead, his first son Rām Rāi. Rām Rāi practically betrayed his own ड़थेर्. Hence the गुरु was obliged to bequeath his seat before passing away to his younger son Harkiṣan, though he was hardly five years old, in 1661.
See also SIKHISM.

Hariścandra
------------------------------------------
In Hindu religion and society, the name ‘Hariścandra’ has become synonymous with सत्य or truth, so much so, that he is called ‘Satya-हरिश्चन्द्र’.
The various legends we come across in our religious literature probably refer to more than one हरिश्चन्द्र. The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (7.18) gives the story of one हरिश्चन्द्र. He was a king of the इक्ष्वाकु dynasty. He had no children. He prayed to वरुण that if he got a son, he would sacrifice him to वरुण. Though a son was born—he was named ‘Rohitāśva’—he went on delaying the sacrifice. Hence वरुण made him ill. To get rid of it, हरिश्चन्द्र bought a ब्राह्मण boy, शुनश्शेफ by name, and tried to sacrifice him to वरुण. However, the pathetic prayers of this boy melted the heart of वरुण who got him released. The boy was adopted by the sage विश्वामित्र who was conducting the sacrifice for हरिश्चन्द्र.
The more common and widely current story of हरिश्चन्द्र runs like this:
The sage वसिष्ठ had declared that the king हरिश्चन्द्र of solar dynasty, son of त्रिशङ्कु was the most truthful person on earth. विश्वामित्र, who could not bear his bete noire’s confidence in हरिश्चन्द्र, vowed to disprove it. Due to his malicious machinations, हरिश्चन्द्र lost his kingdom and wealth, was banished and forced to go to काशी. There, he had to sell his wife Candramati and son Rohitāśva to a rich man to pay his dues to the sage. Then he took employment under the care-taker of a crematory as his assistant. His son Rohitāśva died of snake-bite one day. His wife Candramati was charged with murder by the local king. She was sentenced to death and was brought to the च्रेमतिओन् ground. And, हरिश्चन्द्र had to behead her! As he was about to strike, gods and sages appeared on the scene, prevented it, brought Rohitāśva back to life and restored the kingdom to Hariś-चन्द्र. विश्वामित्र had to concede defeat.

harikathā
(‘stories related to God’)
------------------------------------------
The vast masses of Hindu India, though unlettered or uneducated in the formal sense, have been more educated and cultured than their counterparts in many other countries of the world. This has been mainly due to the methods of mass एदुचतिओन् adopted by the religio-cultural teachers of medieval and post-medieval India.
One of such methods is the हरिकथा found mostly in South India. Kathā-kāla-kṣepa or कालक्षेप (of Tamil Nadu), कीर्तन by the buvās (of Maharashtra), हरिकथा and burrakathā (of Andhra Pradesh) and kathakathā or gīti-ālekhya (of Bengal) are its equivalents.
The main purpose of the हरिकथा is to spread moral, ethical, religious and spiritual ideas among the masses. This is done through the recitation of interesting and touching stories and episodes from the epics, the पुराणस् and the lives of saints.
After preliminary prayers, the Bhāgavatar, as the narrator is generally called, starts either with a song pregnant with a deep philosophy of life or with a short account of some fundamental religio-ethical teaching. The teaching is then expanded and is expounded in detail through the story chosen for the discourse.
Apart from devotional मुसिच्, the narrator also embellishes his discourse with suitable stories and anecdotes interspersed with dramatisation at appropriate places.
The Bhāgavatar is accompanied by musical instruments like the tānpūra, harmonium and tabla or mṛdaṅga (percussion instruments) and ताल (cymbals).
Harikathās spread over 2 to 3 hours’ duration are common and popular even today.
Temples and religious institutions are their patrons.
Modernisation, the result of the fast development of science and technology, has caught up with this art also. Training institutions are coming up where the future Bhāgavatars are receiving training. Audio and video tapes of the Harikathās of the well-known exponents are also being made available to the interested public.

Harimandir
(‘House of God’)
------------------------------------------
Sikhism is the youngest of world religions and was started by गुरु Nānak (A. D. 1469-1539). The हरिमन्दिर्, also called ‘Śrī Darbār Sāhib,’ but popularly known as the ‘Golden Temple’, is the most sacred shrine of the Sikhs. It is in Amritsar (Punjab).
It is situated inside a huge tank the construction of which had been started in A. D. 1577 by गुरु Rāmdās (A. D. 1534-1581). The foundation for the temple was laid by the Muslim saint Mia Mīr (A. D. 1550-1635) in A. D. 1588, at the request of गुरु Arjan (A. D. 1563-1606).
Golden Temple at AmritsarThe dimensions of the tank are 154.5 by 148.5 metres (507 by 487 feet). The temple itself is 12.25 metres (40 feet) square and stands on a platform which is 19.7 metres (64 feet) square.
The temple took its present shape and form during the reign of Mahārājā Raṇjit Singh (A. D. 1780-1839). The architecture is a mixture of the Rajput and the Mughal styles.
The object of worship is the Ādi Granth, (or Guru Granth Sāhib), the sacred scripture of the Sikhs compiled by the fifth गुरु, Arjan. He also set the daily routine and liturgy which continue even today. As in some हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस् where the उत्सवमूर्ति (processional image) is shifted ceremonially in the night to a rest-room, the Book is also reverently escorted from the main shrine to the Akāl Buṅgā (the edifice raised over the Akāl Takht, the primary Church of Sikh religious authority) in the night and brought back in the early morning.
The हरिमन्दिर् has been desecrated several times by hosts of Muslim marauders from Delhi and Afghanistan. They have even defiled the tank in abominable ways including filling it up with sand . However, these sacrilegious acts have always been met with stiff resis-tance and the shrine has been redeemed and renovated with greater vigour and faith.
The great dome over the temple is covered with plates of copper gilded with gold. Hence the name ‘Golden Temple’.
Inside the temple, several verses from the Guru Granth Sāhib (Ādi Granth) have been inscribed in letters of gold on the arches.
See also NĀNAK and SIKHISM.
